questions.question: What is the probability that a teenage driver chosen at random will have a reaction time less than 0.65 seconds?
questions.context: Suppose the reaction times of teenage drivers are normally distributed with a mean of 0.53 seconds and a standard deviation of 0.11 seconds.

questions.question: Find the probability that a teenage driver chosen at random will have a reaction time between 0.4 and 0.6 seconds.
questions.context: Suppose the reaction times of teenage drivers are normally distributed with a mean of 0.53 seconds and a standard deviation of 0.11 seconds.

questions.question: Confidence intervals are a function of which of the following three things?
options: The population, the sample, and the standard deviation
The sample, the variable of interest, and the degrees of freedom
The data in the sample, the confidence level, and the sample size
The sampling distribution, the confidence level, and the degrees of freedom
The mean, the median, and the mode

questions.question: The Mean Squares (MS) for Material Type, Temperature, Interaction (MT × Temperature), and Error are:
questions.context: The effective life, in hours, of batteries is compared by material type (1, 2, or 3) and operating temperature: Low (-10°C), Medium (20°C), or High (45°C). Twelve batteries are randomly selected from each material type and randomly allocated to the temperature levels (4 batteries per cell, total N = 36). Significance level: α = 0.05.

questions.question: The F-values for Material Type, Temperature, and MT × Temperature, respectively, are:
questions.context: A two-way ANOVA is conducted on battery life across 3 Material Types and 3 Temperatures (N = 36, α = 0.05). The computed Mean Squares are: MS(Material Type) = 5341.861, MS(Temperature) = 19559.361, MS(MT × Temperature) = 2405.444, and MS(Error) = 675.213.

questions.question: Is there strong evidence that the mean battery life varies with the material used?
questions.context: In the battery life experiment (α = 0.05), the test statistic for Material Type is F = 7.911, compared against critical F(0.05, 2, 27) = 3.35.

questions.question: A sample of size n = 25 is drawn from a normally distributed population with unknown population standard deviation. Which distribution should be used to construct a confidence interval for the population mean?
questions.context: Sampling distributions and confidence intervals analysis.
options: The t distribution with 24 degrees of freedom

questions.question: Suppose a die is tossed. What is the probability that the die will land on a number that is greater than 5?
If you increase the confidence level, the confidence interval ______.
options: may increase or decrease, depending on the sample data

questions.question: When we replace σ with the sample standard deviation s, we introduce a new source of variability and the sampling distribution becomes the ______.
Construct a 99% confidence interval for the average of the time differences (d = Method A - Method B).
questions.context: The same eleven workers performed a task using two different methods (Method A and Method B). The completion times, in minutes, for each worker are given below.

questions.question: The sample standard deviation of differences, s, is:
questions.context: The same eleven workers performed a task using Method A and Method B. The paired time differences (d = A - B) for the 11 workers are: [0.7, -0.2, 0.4, 0.0, -0.4, 0.9, 0.1, 0.0, 0.6, 0.5, 0.8] with mean d̄ = 0.309 minutes.

questions.question: Based on this confidence interval, there is no significant difference between the results from the two methods.
questions.context: For the eleven workers evaluated under Method A and Method B, the 99% confidence interval for the mean time difference is (-0.104, 0.722) minutes.

questions.question: Can the professor have 90% confidence that the mean score for the class on the test would be at least 70?
questions.context: A professor wants to know if her introductory statistics class has a good grasp of basic mathematics. Six students chosen at random from the class obtain scores of 62, 92, 75, 68, 83, and 95 on a math proficiency test. The target score is μ₀ = 70 with a 90% confidence level (α = 0.10, df = 5).

questions.question: The critical value in the t-table (t₀.₁₀,₅) and the calculated test statistic (t), respectively, are:
questions.context: Six students scored 62, 92, 75, 68, 83, and 95 (sample mean x̄ = 79.17, sample standard deviation s = 13.17, sample size n = 6, test threshold μ₀ = 70 at α = 0.10, one-tailed with df = 5).

questions.question: When an analysis of variance is performed on samples drawn from k populations, the mean square between treatments is:
The following are features of Latin Square Designs, except:
options: They handle the case when we have several nuisance factors and we either cannot combine them into a single factor or wish to keep them separate.
They allow experiments with a relatively small number of runs.
The number of levels of each blocking variable must equal the number of levels of the treatment factor.
The Latin square model assumes that there are no interactions between the blocking variables or between the treatment variable and the blocking variables.
They are equivalent to specific fractional factorial designs.

questions.question: The sums of squares between detergents (SS_between), within detergents (SS_within), and total (SS_total), respectively, are:
questions.context: In a comparison of the cleaning action of four detergents (A, B, C, D), soiled pieces of white cloth were washed under controlled conditions. Seventeen pieces of cloth were measured for whiteness across the 4 detergents. Assume all whiteness readings are normally distributed with common variance (α = 0.05, k = 4, N = 17).

questions.question: The F-ratio is:
questions.context: In the four-detergent comparison (N = 17, k = 4), the sums of squares are SS(between) = 216.67 (df = 3) and SS(within) = 873.80 (df = 13), giving MS(between) = 72.22 and MS(within) = 67.22.

questions.question: Is there evidence, at the 5% significance level, to suggest a difference between the four brands as regards the mean whiteness after washing?
questions.context: In the detergent experiment, the calculated F-ratio is 1.07, and the critical value at the 5% significance level is F(0.05, 3, 13) = 3.41.

questions.question: What is the probability that a randomly selected factory worker can assemble the part in under 75 seconds or in over 81 seconds?
questions.context: A consultant determined that the time, in seconds, to assemble a part for workers trained with a particular method was normally distributed with a mean of 75 seconds and a standard deviation of 6 seconds.

questions.question: The null and alternative hypotheses to test whether the team differs from national average are:
questions.context: A Little League baseball coach wants to know if his team is representative of other teams in scoring runs. Nationally, the average number of runs scored by a Little League team in a game is 5.7. He chooses five games at random in which his team scored 5, 9, 4, 11, and 8 runs (n = 5, α = 0.05).
options: H₀: μ = 5.7 and H₁: μ < 5.7 and μ > 5.7

questions.question: The sample standard deviation, s, is:
questions.context: A Little League baseball team scored 5, 9, 4, 11, and 8 runs across five randomly selected games (n = 5, sample mean x̄ = 7.4 runs, national average μ = 5.7).

questions.question: Can the coach conclude that his team is significantly different from the national distribution on runs scored?
questions.context: For the Little League team scoring 5, 9, 4, 11, and 8 runs (n = 5, x̄ = 7.4, s = 2.89, national μ = 5.7, α = 0.05), the calculated test statistic is t = 1.32 and the two-tailed critical value is t(0.025, 4) = 2.776.

questions.question: The hypotheses to test whether a significant difference exists between younger and older adults are:
questions.context: A research study examined differences between older adults (> 70 yrs, n₁ = 10) and younger adults (20–30 yrs, n₂ = 10) on life satisfaction (scale 0–60, where higher scores indicate greater satisfaction). Test at α = 0.05.
options: H₀: μ₁ = μ₂ and H₁: μ₁ > μ₂
H₀: μ₁ − μ₂ = 0 and H₁: μ₁ ≠ μ₂
H₀: μ₁ = μ₂ and H₁: μ₁ < μ₂
H₀: μ₁ − μ₂ = 0 and H₁: μ₁ < μ₂

questions.question: The sample standard deviations, s₁ (younger) and s₂ (older), are:
questions.context: Ten younger adults had scores [34, 22, 15, 27, 37, 41, 24, 19, 26, 36] (x̄₁ = 28.10) and ten older adults had scores [45, 38, 52, 48, 25, 39, 51, 46, 55, 46] (x̄₂ = 44.50).

questions.question: The two-sample independent t statistic is:
questions.context: For younger adults (n₁ = 10, x̄₁ = 28.10, s₁ = 8.68) and older adults (n₂ = 10, x̄₂ = 44.50, s₂ = 8.54) with pooled standard error SE = 3.85.

questions.question: Did older adults in this sample have significantly higher life satisfaction than younger adults?
questions.context: In the life satisfaction study comparing older adults (x̄₂ = 44.50) vs younger adults (x̄₁ = 28.10), the calculated t-statistic is t = 4.258, which exceeds the critical value t(0.025, 18) = 2.101 at α = 0.05.

questions.question: The Sum of Squares (SS) for Position, Rabbit, and Order, respectively, are:
questions.context: The skins of four rabbits were inoculated with a diffusing factor in four sites (Positions I–IV) in four different orders (a, b, c, d) using a 4×4 Latin Square Design. The measured outcome is blister area (cm²). (Letters in parentheses represent inoculation order).

questions.context: In the Latin Square experiment evaluating inoculation order (df_numerator = 3, df_error = 6), the test statistic for Order is F = 0.467, while the critical value at α = 0.05 is F(0.05, 3, 6) = 4.76.
